The Guisheng was a new ship of the Jardine company, launched only last year from the shipyards of Glasgow, in Britain. She could make sixteen knots an hour; from Guangzhou to Shanghai took her but sixty hours, two days and a half. On this run she was the fastest afloat. Today was the thirteenth of the first month, and the ship had been more than fifty hours at sea.
That noon, the first thing Old Xiao said on waking was: what day of the first month is it today?
It's the tenth of the first month. He let out a breath, relieved, having feared he had lain senseless far longer.
“What in the end became of Comrade Ling Wen?”
He was not yet fully awake; his eyes were clouded, and between his labored breaths he seemed to be straining to call something to mind.
“She has disappeared,” Chen Qianli said softly, “that very day. You told her to come to the liaison station the next day — was there something you had to say to her?”

Old Xiao closed his eyes again, his mouth twisting with pain; after a moment he heaved a long sigh: “Lin Shi never came, and neither did she. This matter is too important — even if one is to die for it, it must be seen through before one dies.”
Chen Qianli knew they had not much time; he must learn the whole of it quickly. He gave Mo Shaoqiu a look, and Mo Shaoqiu rose, lifted the door-curtain, and went out.
In the shack Chen Qianli spoke, low, a passage of code — the same he had used before when making contact with Lin Shi, a cipher that Comrade Shaoshan had devised himself.
As he had expected, Old Xiao knew the code. The instant he spoke the last line of it, Old Xiao's eyes lit up; with difficulty he turned his head and gave him a long, deep look.

Old Xiao said that he had been charged by Comrade Shaoshan to deliver a message to Lin Shi in person. The message contained an advertisement, which must be printed in the newspaper on the fourteenth of the first month. Besides the daily paper, should anything go amiss, it was to run once more in that afternoon's evening edition. Word for word he recited the advertisement twice over, and told Chen Qianli that the advertisement was in truth a contact signal, and that the other party was Comrade Haohan. After the advertisement a telephone number was to be appended; once Comrade Haohan saw the notice he would dial that number, and whoever answered was to tell Haohan the place and time of the meeting, and, the meeting once made, to cover his withdrawal from Shanghai at once.

For the present Comrade Haohan had gone swiftly underground, severing every working tie. After his last wireless exchange with Ruijin he had shifted into hiding, where none could reach him again; he waited only for the agreed contact signal to appear in the papers.
But the train of upheavals Old Xiao met with after reaching Guangzhou had led him in the end to entrust this task to Yi Junnian.

In fact it was at that very moment that Chen Qianli realized Yi Junnian might not be what he seemed. In some corner of his mind there lay stored an old matter — a riddle he would have given all he had to solve, the answer to a question. To learn that answer, Ye Tao had given her life.

Old Xiao held on to consciousness with all his strength. He got the account out in broken snatches, a few sentences and then a pause to catch his breath, then beginning again; on certain crucial points, fearing that his head might swim and he would say it wrong, he repeated himself several times over. Chen Qianli for his part was very still, making not the least sound from first to last, neither pressing him nor putting questions. He knew that in Old Xiao's present state, to speak all this to the end must have cost a vast effort of will.

Afterward Chen Qianli and Liang Shichao went to Haoxian Road, learned a few things by inquiry on Weixin North Road, and then went on to the Lehua Theatre. Coming out of the theatre they returned to the liaison station, where Mo Shaoqiu had spent the whole afternoon contriving to get two tickets on the fastest boat. Tickets in hand, they boarded that same night. The ship sailed at twelve, in the dead of night.

The second-class double cabin was up above the deck, with an upper and a lower berth; Liang Shichao was sleeping like a log. Guangdong man though he was, his old home lay in the mountains of the north of the province, and he could not swim a stroke; with wind and waves high in the night, he had climbed into the upper berth and dropped off at once, giddy and dazed.

That Liang Shichao and Ling Wen should go to Guangzhou had been Lin Shi's idea; but at the time Chen Qianli had had a dim feeling of his own that to let Yi Junnian and Ling Wen make the journey together might lay bare a riddle that had haunted him for years. In that year long past, it was in seeking that same answer that Ye Tao had fallen at last beneath the enemy's guns. He had not then truly taken up the work; he understood little of communism, and nothing of the intricacy of secret work. Nor did he understand why the passing-on of a single sentence could matter so much as to be worth a life.

That year she was but twenty-three. He remembered it clearly: it was on her birthday — the fifteenth of the first month — that he reached Nanjing. Parted from her nearly a year, he saw her again, and her father too, his teacher Ye Qinian.

In the years when Ye Qinian was still a university professor, an anarchist, a scholar of Esperanto, Chen Qianli, like many a young man, had once believed that for most of the questions that perplexed one, Teacher Ye had the answers. The talk among the students grew by degrees into a legend — of that house of Teacher Ye's on Xinzha Road, and of a secret society within it. Those were the ardent, revolutionary years of the twenties, when every young man was high in spirit and burning to join some organization or other.

Only a chosen few among the students had the luck to be admitted there. It was Teacher Ye's home: the family lived upstairs, the ground floor served for receiving guests, and the society and its magazine were on the ground floor too. Later, when Chen Qianli repeated to Teacher Ye the legend that ran along the school corridors, Ye Qinian laughed and said that an air of mystery was a useful weapon in its own right. For a while he went to Xinzha Road every day, sitting by the long table listening to the grand talk, helping the magazine with odd jobs, carrying letters here and there and handing out documents; he had even transported explosives (though those anarchist bombs never went off anywhere at all).

It was a long time before he first saw Ye Tao. It was a sweltering afternoon; slogans were pasted up along the streets, and strikes of workers and shopkeepers were breaking out everywhere. She was sitting in the ground-floor parlor, and at first he took her wrongly for someone belonging to the society; only afterward did he learn she was Teacher Ye's daughter, who had never appeared before because she was a student at the Beijing Women's Normal University. That summer the school had been closed down by the Duan Qirui government and its students forcibly dispersed, and so she had come back to Shanghai.

Ye Qinian had been wrong all along: look at it how you would, it was not Chen Qianli who had led Ye Tao onto that road of opposition to her father. The truth was the very reverse — it was Ye Tao who had been Chen Qianli's guide. It was Ye Tao who told him that behind her father's nihilism there lurked an opportunist and a careerist.

One day Ye Qinian called him into the study and told him, with great gravity, that henceforth he was not to go into Ye Tao's room as he pleased. It was precisely under these circumstances that a certain bewitching confusion at last dissolved — like a gust of wind passing, like sunlight melting the mist-frost from the glass — and he and Ye Tao, the two of them, saw each other's hearts entirely plain.

Then, once more to his surprise, Ye Tao went to Nanjing. At the time he did not yet understand why, disliking so much the things Ye Qinian did, she should have gone and joined in them herself. Only long afterward did he learn that the place she had gone to was the Kuomintang's Party Affairs Investigation Section, where, at her father's arranging, she had become a clerk in the confidential office. And of course he had not then grasped that she went to Nanjing precisely because, in those very years, Ye Qinian was becoming another man. In those years a great many people became another sort of person.

At the time he had asked himself over and over: could it be that Zhaofeng Garden, the setting sun, the early-spring lake-water, the pair of swans upon it — that all this had been only his dreaming? Could the words they had spoken, hands clasped and hearts pounding, have been no more than the impulse of a moment before parting? He had always known well enough that of the two of them it was Ye Tao who was always the first to leave. From the moment he first met her at Teacher Ye's house, she had been leaving him.

In the wing-room upstairs on Xinzha Road he sat beneath the window and she before the dressing table, and as they talked he saw two of her, one before him and one in the mirror. He was wholly lost in their subject, but even as they spoke she rose all at once and hurried out of the house. He heard her speak of The Captain's Daughter, and got hold of the novel too, and only when he had read it came to discuss it with her — whereupon she said she did not care much for the story any more. They went to lectures together; he had only just grasped the grammar when she announced she was leaving the Esperanto class for a Russian one. He was still lost in An Appeal to the Young when she had already begun quietly reading New Youth.

Ye Qinian and his friends argued over Bakunin in the ground-floor parlor on Xinzha Road, and he listened enraptured (such fervor these men had); he and she both sat in a corner of the room, and after some weeks of listening she told him that it was Lenin who had the right of it. He always had the faint sense that somewhere else, in some other place, there must be a more important thing waiting for her.

A year later he too went to Nanjing. He had braced himself to meet Ye Qinian's anger, or his coldness, or some more insidious stratagem. But ever since Ye Tao had come to work at her father's side, Ye Qinian had seemed to feel he need trouble over her no longer. Perhaps he supposed that in a place swarming with secret agents and intrigue Ye Tao would soon enough change her view of the world. But in any case, relax his guard or not, Ye Qinian was simply too busy. In those days he often flew to Guangzhou, seeming taken up with the laying of some plan.

Chen Qianli rented a small room in Shipopo Lane. By day he did translations for a publishing house and waited for Ye Tao to come off work. Sometimes she telephoned him (there was a public telephone at the cigarette-and-paper shop at the lane's mouth) and had him come to the place where she worked (before long he knew it for the Kuomintang's Party Affairs Investigation Section); she would set him little errands too — to buy a packet of sweets at such-and-such a shop, or fetch some clothes from the tailor's.

So long as Ye Qinian was away from Nanjing, the Zhanyuan was for Ye Tao a place of perfect freedom. It was a great garden, said to have been a princely mansion in the old days, with a spirit-screen before its gate and rockeries within. The confidential office lay at the garden's far north; past the rockery one could see that row of single-story houses. When he arrived he would have the gatekeeper telephone through, and Ye Tao would come out to meet him; sometimes the gatekeeper would show him in, and in the end the gatekeeper simply let him go in by himself. In memory those few months passed in a peculiar peace, and Ye Tao was peculiarly happy. She seemed to have found work that truly interested her.

He found that Ye Tao was closer to him now than before. The two of them were three years apart in age, and before this she had been more like an elder sister; but after the year's interval things seemed somewhat altered — perhaps at this stage he had, on the contrary, grown up a little faster than she.

They went to Plum Blossom Hill; it was early spring, the second month, and plum blossoms had opened all along the gnarled boughs, so that the hillside seemed wrapped in a pink mist. Heart answering to heart, they felt the whole world draw off into the distance, leaving before their eyes only the plum trees, the blue sky, and that one face. Full of gladness, they recited Nekrasov together: They say a storm is coming — and I cannot help but smile.

But the world was still here, and the setting Ye Tao stood in the midst of was a dangerous one. The Zhanyuan held many a grim, hard-faced man, wolfhounds, guns, papers no one was allowed to touch, warning boards forbidding entry. From behind the rockery in the north of the garden there came, now and then, a scream or two. Later, up on Qixia Hill, Ye Tao told him that this was the Party Affairs Investigation Section, a world of intrigue and killing that Ye Qinian had had a hand in building.

It was not until that last month that he came to know what work she was really doing, though he had guessed something of it earlier. Looking back now, it may be that she had been hinting to him all along, quietly telling him the truth: that what she truly did was secret work, work that meant a great deal to her. And in his own heart he understood well that the things she did were very likely aimed at wrecking her father's. But before she let him know the truth, she had already pointed him the way, had shown him what kind of cause a person must throw himself into to make a life mean more.

She had never truly left him; even after going to Nanjing she wrote to him every few days, and those letters carried on the clash of ideas from before. Only now did he understand that in writing them she had run some little risk, and that it was lucky she worked at the Zhanyuan, where she had means to keep the letters from falling into the hands of the postal censors. She had books and magazines sent to him too, by this hand and that: The Communist Manifesto, Letters from Afar, The Bolshevik, and the volume of Nekrasov's poems she loved.

The day before the Dragon Boat Festival, Ye Tao telephoned the cigarette-and-paper shop in Shipopo Lane. In those days he seldom saw her; she seemed busy the whole day long, and even when she did see him she was very silent, and if he asked too much she would flare up all at once. Over the telephone Ye Tao told him to come to the Zhanyuan, and to stop first, on the way, at the Chengnan teahouse-and-cake shop by the Qinhuai River and buy her a packet of Minnan tangerine-red cakes. Ye Tao had always been fond of nibbling on sweets; in Shanghai he had often run such errands for her, and though in Nanjing many of her old habits had fallen away, this fondness for sweets stayed just as it was. Besides this shop's tangerine-red cakes and its crisp sugar-candy, she was fond too of a certain peddler's osmanthus-sugar taro shoots, always cried for sale in the neighborhood of the Zhanyuan's gate.

He bought the tangerine-red cakes, but at the gate of the Zhanyuan he was stopped. To all appearances the Zhanyuan was an ordinary old house — the paint on its gate on Daoshu Street was flaked and worn — yet in the gatehouse there always sat one or two burly men in Zhongshan tunics. These months past the several shifts of gatekeepers at the two gates, south-front and north-back, had all come to know him, and seeing him come in they hastened to telephone the confidential office for Clerk Ye. Ye Tao told the gatekeeper that today she could not leave the secure area, and had him register the visit and let Chen Qianli go in by himself. In the courtyard behind the gate stood a spirit-screen; turning past it, one came to a pool where water-lilies floated and fish swam, its edge carried on stone piers as a covered walk; behind the walk was a rockery, and the rockery had a grotto, and climbing the steps up through the grotto one could sit in the little pavilion at its summit and look out across to the Qinhuai River.

Chen Qianli, having come so often, had long known that behind the rockery in the north of the garden lay the so-called secure area, where at every step one might be under watch and neither person nor thing could pass in or out at will. But he was “Clerk Ye's” — that is, the eldest young lady of Director Ye's household's — young man, and for the most part those who saw him pretended not to. In that row of single-story houses that was the confidential office Chen Qianli found Ye Tao. She ate one of the tangerine-red cakes and said: how is it these cakes are so dry today? How long have they been sitting about? — and threw it aside in vexation, and gave him the cold shoulder for a good while, the two other women in the office smiling at him in sympathy. After a time Ye Tao called to him again: “Go to the gate and buy me a bowl of osmanthus-sugar taro shoots, will you.”

When he had just come in, Chen Qianli had not seen any peddler crying his wares at the Zhanyuan's gate. But he said nothing; every time Ye Tao sent him to the gate to buy osmanthus-sugar taro shoots, that peddler would always be there.
“If you don't see him, run on ahead to Mafu Street; he's usually in one place or another around there.”

He came out carrying the vacuum flask, the gatekeeper smiling at him. Out of the Zhanyuan, sure enough, there was the peddler's carrying-pole. The peddler lifted the lid and set it aside, ladled a few spoonfuls of the red, fragrant taro pottage from his great pot into the flask, scattered in a pinch of powdered osmanthus, then took up a cloth to wipe the lid, capped it, and took the money. Chen Qianli carried the sugared taro shoots into the confidential office; Ye Tao took a sip, and only then did a satisfied smile appear on her face.

It was some days later that he learned there had been a slip of paper under the flask's lid, and on it urgent intelligence. Without knowing it he had carried that intelligence out. Ye Qinian had broken up the Communist underground in Guangzhou and arrested Ouyang Min, the head of the Guangdong underground Party. Because the intelligence had been got out in time, the higher Party organs in contact with Ouyang Min had all withdrawn.

By the time he knew of all this, Ye Tao already lay gravely wounded. She told Chen Qianli that she was a member of the Communist Party; she had not told him before because she had been placed by the Party organization to lie hidden within the Kuomintang's Party Affairs Investigation Section and had had to keep the secret, but now she could tell him.

She said she had meant all along to bring him into the Party, but that now she had no time left; she hoped that one day he would become a staunch communist fighter. She told him that because she had passed on word of Ouyang Min's arrest in good time, the organization had moved quickly, clearing out the offices ahead of the agents and getting away most of the comrades on the arrest list. From this Ye Qinian came to suspect that there was a leak within the Party Affairs Investigation Section.

She ought to have kept still a while, but she could not help opening Ye Qinian's safe once again. For her superiors had put a question to her — had Ouyang Min turned traitor? — and so she had to find the answer. Ye Tao had once dreamed with him of the future: in a few more days they would leave the Zhanyuan together, leave Nanjing. She would lead him to a place full of light and hope.

Ye Tao found the answer, but she was killed on the way to deliver the word. Before she died she charged Chen Qianli to carry one sentence to the Party: Ouyang Min has turned traitor. Yet precisely because she had been discovered by the enemy in the act of getting the intelligence out, another possibility remained: that the enemy had deliberately misled her with false information. Later, word came from Guangzhou that Ouyang Min too was dead — the enemy had shot him. On the day of the execution all his fellow prisoners watched him marched out of the cells. Afterward the organization had sent someone to look into it, had even ventured to make inquiries at the Public Security Bureau, but the end of it was nothing at all.

He had never for a moment believed there was anything wrong with the intelligence she had sent out — to obtain it Ye Tao had given her very life. For three years the question had haunted his mind, and often he turned it about the other way: if Ouyang Min was a traitor, why should Ye Qinian have killed him? To kill a man might be only to silence him, to cover up some plot.

What sort of plot, then, could make Ye Qinian think it worth killing a turncoat like Ouyang Min? A traitor of Ouyang Min's kind ought to have been of great value in Ye Qinian's eyes. He was the head of the Communist underground, with a mass of working ties inside the organization; he knew a great many people and was privy to many secrets. There would be much he might not yet have called to mind in the first few interrogations — for though a man turning his coat is surely eager to tell the enemy all he knows, he always leaves something out. Even after he had been squeezed clean as a tube of toothpaste, wrung to an empty roll of foil, he could still be made to write shameless things for the papers. The Special Operations Headquarters did indeed have a department given over to what they called “psychological warfare,” concocting rumors and spreading them abroad. Why, then, this haste to kill him? What, in the end, had Ye Qinian gained by shooting Ouyang Min?
Now he knew.
